release_schedule.note: This is a one-off legal/regulatory instrument (EAC Regulations for Compiling Harmonised Consumer Price Indices, published March 2022), not a recurring statistical publication. The document itself was 'gazetted' with a target entry-into-force date of 31 Dec 2024 (Article 106), a one-time milestone, not a recurring cycle. Internally it does specify review cycles for the underlying CPI methodology (weights reviewed at max 5-year intervals per Art. 704.1, mini-surveys every 2-3 years per Art. 704.2, EAC-level weights every 3-5 years per Art. 706.5, annual compliance reports per Art. 113.3), but none of these are a stated periodicity for reissuing or amending the Regulations document itself. There is no found evidence of a fixed amendment/republication cadence for the Regulations text, so releases_per_year probably should not be treated as a fixed number for this report at all -- it is better modeled as irregular (amended only when the EAC Council/Secretariat decides to revise it) rather than assigned any specific interval.

Nqazidja [Ngazidja] / 27,4%... Ndzouani / 25,7%... Mwali / 9,4%'. Those four figures match this organic law's Article 8 formula exactly (Union 37,50% / Ngazidja 27,4% / Anjouan 25,7% / Mohéli 9,4%), and Article 7 of the organic law states the mechanism 'ne peut être modifié que par une loi organique' (can only be amended by [another] organic law) -- i.e. the annual finance law's residual-split percentages are calculated per this organic law's formula, not independently set each year. Note this is distinct from the separate 1,85%-of-internal-revenue 'gouvernorats' pooled-transfer mechanism in the 2026 edition's own Article 4, which is a different, smaller allocation than the Article 8 residual-quote-part split.

targetReport.title: Loi organique N°05-001/AU du 16 janvier 2005 fixant la quote-part des recettes publiques à partager entre l'Union et les Îles Autonomes
targetReport.publisher: Assemblée de l'Union des Comores / Ministère de la Justice des Comores
targetReport.description: The organic law establishing the formula for splitting non-retroceded public revenues between the Union government and the three Autonomous Islands (Ngazidja/Grande Comore, Anjouan, Mohéli). Adopted by the Assemblée de l'Union on 16 January 2005 and promulgated by Décret N°05-023/PR (30 March 2005, President Azali Assoumani). Hosted as a full 4-page, 9-article PDF directly on justice.gouv.km, the Comorian Ministry of Justice's own legal-texts portal (HTTP 200, pdftotext-verified). Article 1 sets the underlying distinction: "La loi de finances de l'Union des Comores conformément aux alinéas 1 et 3 de l'article 11 de la constitution rétrocède directement au profit des budgets des Iles Autonomes les recettes publiques devant être recouvrées et utilisées par ces dernières. Ces recettes publiques sont dites recettes propres des Iles Autonomes. Les ressources non rétrocédées directement au profit des budgets des Iles Autonomes seront à partager entre l'Union et les Iles Autonomes suivant les dispositions de la présente loi organique." Article 8 states the operative quote-part formula: "la quote-part est fixée, après déduction des charges de la dette publique et des contributions aux organismes internationaux, des prestations de services et des pensions comme suit : - Union : 37,50% ; - Ngazidja : 27,4% ; - Anjouan : 25,7%; - Mohéli: 9,4%." Article 7 states the amendment procedure: "Le Gouverneur de la Banque Centrale est tenu de respecter scrupuleusement ce mécanisme qui ne peut être modifié que par une loi organique." Signed by Le Président de l'Assemblée de l'Union, Said Dhoiffir Bounou, and Secretaries Bacar Abdou / Bacar Houmadi. CONSTITUTIONAL-BASIS NOTE: the law's own Article 1 cites "l'article 11 de la constitution de l'Union des Comores du 23 Décembre 2001" (as originally numbered), not the 'Article 104' a prior round (AF/G.23) had hypothesized -- see _dropped for why no edge is drawn to km-constitution-union-2001 this round. Corroborated (secondary, not primary) by a verbatim-identical reproduction of Décret N°05-023/PR at comoresdroit.comores-droit.com (private Comorian legal-reference site) and by a 2013 PEFA assessment (pefa.org) stating the mechanism was still described as operative as of 2013: "Une loi organique fixe la quote-part des recettes publiques devant respectivement revenir à l'Union et aux Îles."

targetReport.description: Four named corporate and unincorporated tax returns that substitute for survey responses across the Integrated Business Statistics Program. IMDB record 2103 states both the mechanism and the motive: 'A strategy to replace survey data with tax data has been introduced to reduce the respondent burden and survey costs... As part of the Integrated Business Statistics Program (IBSP), T1 tax data are used for unincorporated businesses, T2 tax data for incorporated businesses, T3010 tax data for registered charities and T5013 tax data for partnerships. release_schedule.note: The corpus URL (StatCan IMDB SDDS=2103) is the survey page for the Annual Survey of Manufacturing and Logging Industries (ASML), one of several annual business surveys under the Integrated Business Statistics Program (IBSP). That page carries the exact boilerplate passage matching this report's title: 'As part of the Integrated Business Statistics Program (IBSP), T1 tax data are used for unincorporated businesses, T2 tax data for incorporated businesses, T3010 tax data for registered charities and T5013 tax data for partnerships.' This same administrative-tax-data description appears generically across many IBSP survey pages (it describes a data-collection method, not a standalone dated publication), so there is no single dedicated 'tax data' release calendar. The dated releases actually shown on this page (for 2024 reference-year data: December 18, 2025 and March 27, 2026) both fall before today (2026-08-11). Reference-period collection runs April-August of the year after the reference year, with a first release the following December and a revision the following March -- an annual pattern. Projecting that pattern forward gives an expected release around December 2026 (for 2025 reference-year data) with a follow-up revision around March 2027. These are inferred/projected dates, not dates published on a forward-looking calendar.

targetReport.title: Monthly Survey of Manufacturing (MSM)
targetReport.description: Monthly survey of Canadian manufacturing sales, inventories, unfilled orders and capacity utilisation, IMDB record 2101. Named as an indicator source by the monthly GDP-by-industry programme for most manufacturing industries, and named alongside the IPPI in the deflation rows of that programme's source table. The target population is drawn from the Business Register and classified by NAICS: 'The target population for the MSM consists of all statistical establishments on the Business Register that are classified to the manufacturing sector (by NAICS), which are categorized into over 156 industries.' Sales for low-revenue establishments are derived from GST files rather than collected, which is an administrative input with no publication behind it.
targetReport.cadence_note: Monthly. Record 2101 states 'Frequency: Monthly'. Two things about the historical record are worth keeping: the MSM was benchmarked to the Annual Survey of Manufacturing and Logging only 'up to and including 2003', so that specific arrangement has not held for two decades, and the present-tense relationship in the other direction is stated by the annual survey's own record rather than by this one.

targetReport.title: Annual Survey of Manufacturing and Logging Industries (ASML)
targetReport.description: Annual census-and-sample survey of establishments primarily engaged in manufacturing and logging, IMDB record 2103. It is the annual anchor for the manufacturing side of the Canadian accounts and it names its own consumers in its own words: 'Within Statistics Canada, the data are used by the Canadian System of National Accounts, the Monthly Survey of Manufacturing (record number 2101) and Prices programs.' That sentence is the only present-tense statement of the ASML-to-MSM relationship found; the MSM's own record describes the arrangement in the past tense and dates it to 2003. Survey data are substituted with T1, T2, T3010 and T5013 tax data under the Integrated Business Statistics Program, which is an administrative input with no publication behind it. The IPPI's own record 2318 names the 2019 ASML as one of two weighting sources, which is why this node is worth more than a manufacturing statistic normally would be.

This series is the practical way most sub-national fiscal data enter the national statistical system and downstream analyses.

targetReport.title: National Pensions Act, 1992 (Act No. 10 of 1992)
targetReport.publisher: Government of the Republic of Namibia
targetReport.description: Namibia's foundational statute for the universal old-age pension, read section-by-section this session via NamibLII. VERIFIED DIRECTLY. Purpose: 'to provide for national pensions to be paid to aged, blind and disabled persons' (Social Protection Policy 2021-2030's own citation of the Act, p.15, s.5.3, quoted verbatim: 'The National Pensions Act, 1992 (No. 10 of 1992), provides for national pensions to be paid to aged, visually impaired and persons with disability, and to provide for matters incidental thereto'). On amount-setting, s.16(1)(b) assigns 'the payment of national pensions including the maximum amount to be paid, the determination of the amount to be paid in any particular case' to ministerial regulation; s.16(3) permits 'different pensions to be paid to different categories of aged persons according to their income and other assets'; s.16(2) requires parliamentary approval only for reductions to aggregate pension entitlements. The Minister acts 'in consultation with the Minister of Finance'. No section ties any amount to the Consumer Price Index or any price index -- the mechanism is explicitly ministerial/regulatory discretion, not an absence of a stated mechanism.

results.basis: Local Authorities Act 23 of 1992, s.77(1)-(2): 'There shall be levied for the benefit of the funds of regional councils an amount equal to five per cent of the rates levied under section 73 on all rateable property situated in local authority areas. ... The amount referred to in subsection (1) shall be collected by a local authority council situated in the region of the regional council concerned ... and paid over to the regional council.' A regional council's funds under Regional Councils Act s.33(1)(a) ('moneys appropriated by law for purposes of the funds of the regional council') include this amount, which is mechanically computed as a fixed 5% of the local-authority property rates levied under the Local Authorities Act s.73 -- the clearest documented municipal-to-regional fiscal-transfer formula found in this round's research.

The amount referred to in subsection (1) shall be collected by a local authority council situated in the region of the regional council concerned ... and paid over to the regional council.

targetReport.title: Local Authorities Act 23 of 1992
targetReport.publisher: Government of the Republic of Namibia
targetReport.description: Namibia's foundational statute governing local authority councils (municipalities, towns and villages, e.g. Windhoek, Walvis Bay, Swakopmund), including their finances. VERIFIED DIRECTLY this round via the Legal Assistance Centre's Annotated Statutes edition -- a verbatim reproduction (with bracketed amendment annotations) of the Government Gazette Act text, not an NGO paraphrase. Section 77(1)-(2), Part XVI, establishes the clearest documented municipal-to-regional fiscal-transfer formula found in the Namibian corpus to date: 'There shall be levied for the benefit of the funds of regional councils an amount equal to five per cent of the rates levied under section 73 on all rateable property situated in local authority areas. ... The amount referred to in subsection (1) shall be collected by a local authority council situated in the region of the regional council concerned in such manner as may be determined by the Minister and paid over to the regional council on such date or dates as may be so determined.' Section 80(1), Part XVII ('Financial Matters'), defines a local authority council's own funds: 'The funds of a local authority council shall consist of - (a) moneys appropriated by law for purposes of the funds of the local authority council; (b) the rates, charges, fees and other moneys levied under any provision of this Act and received by the local authority council; ...' -- establishing, without naming a specific grant/subsidy scheme, that local authorities' funds may include national-law appropriations. Hosting caveat: this copy is hosted by the Legal Assistance Centre (lac.org.na), a Namibian NGO, not a .gov.na domain -- every .gov.na domain tested this round (including npc.gov.na) either TLS-reset mid-handshake or returned HTTP 503/404, so no working government-hosted mirror of this Act could be confirmed this round; the LAC copy is a verbatim annotated reproduction of the Act of Parliament text, not a paraphrase.
targetReport.cadence_note: One-off foundational legal instrument, currently in force per this annotated compilation.

targetReport.title: Pension Reform Act, 2014
targetReport.description: Nigeria's framework pension statute. Section 15(4) is quoted directly in PenCom's own December 2025 circular (VERIFIED DIRECTLY this session): 'Section 15(4) of the Pension Reform Act (PRA) 2014 guarantees the right of retirees of the Public Service of the Federation to pension review.' Section 53 is separately invoked, per Grok's round (secondary, via PenCom statements as reported in press coverage, not independently quoted from the Act itself or a primary circular) as the basis for PenCom's enforcement action increasing legacy NSITF pensions -- see ng-nsitf-legacy-pension-enforcement. Neither section prescribes a CPI or inflation-based formula; both require periodic review without specifying the method, leaving quantum and timing to administrative determination -- the same shape as the Constitution's own s.173(3) (quoted in full under ng-pencom-federal-pension-review-circular), which requires review 'every five years or together with any Federal Civil Service salary reviews, whichever is earlier' but not a calculation method.

targetReport.publisher: Ministerie van Binnenlandse Zaken en Koninkrijksrelaties (BZK) / Ministerie van Financiën
targetReport.description: The provincial-level counterpart to the Gemeentefonds — the national equalization transfer to the Netherlands' 12 provinces, distributed under the same Financiële-verhoudingswet (confirmed: wetten.overheid.nl's own list of delegated regulations under the Fvw includes both the Besluit financiële verhouding 2001, whose Bijlage 1 governs provinces and Bijlage 2 governs municipalities, and separate year-specific 'Besluit vaststelling bedragen per eenheid uitkering provinciefonds' decrees).

release_schedule.note: BZK/Financien publish three circulaires per year for the provinciefonds (meicirculaire in late May, septembercirculaire in mid-September, decembercirculaire in December), mirroring the identical schedule for the gemeentefonds. No fixed-date calendar is published in advance; dates are inferred from the consistent pattern of past editions. The septembercirculaire has coincided with Prinsjesdag (the constitutionally fixed third Tuesday of September) in each of the last three years observed (2023-09-19, 2024-09-17, 2025-09-16), so 2026-09-15 (Prinsjesdag 2026) is a high-confidence projection. The decembercirculaire has varied between Dec 12-16 in recent years (2024-12-12, 2025-12-16), and the meicirculaire between May 27-31 (2024-05-27, 2026-05-29), so those two are given month-level precision only.

targetReport.title: Forskrift om rapportering fra kommuner og fylkeskommuner mv. (KOSTRA-forskriften)
targetReport.description: Regulation of 18 October 2019 no. 1412, issued under kommuneloven (Act of 22 June 2018 no. 83) § 16-1 and IKS-loven § 42, prescribing what economic and service data municipalities, county authorities and inter-municipal companies must report and requiring that all KOSTRA reporting be made electronically to Statistics Norway. In force 1 January 2020. The Norwegian functional equivalent of the Dutch BBV/Iv3 reporting rules (nl-bbv) in this corpus.
targetReport.cadence_note: Amended periodically rather than issued as dated editions (e.g. amending regulation FOR-2023-11-04-1859), the same pattern nl-bbv and psab-psas are filed under. Canonical consolidation is on lovdata.no, which is robots.txt-blocked to this pipeline; operative text verified via the ministry's Veileder til KOSTRA-forskriften (regjeringen.no PDF, fetched).

release_schedule.rule: KOSTRA-forskriften § 4, third paragraph: "fristen for å rapportere opplysninger om ressursbruk og tjenester er 15. februar" (deadline for reporting resource-use/service data is 15 February). § 5, third paragraph: "fristen for å rapportere årsregnskapene er senest 22. februar i året etter regnskapsåret" (deadline for submitting annual accounts is no later than 22 February in the year following the accounting year).
release_schedule.note: This is a regulation (forskrift) governing when Norwegian municipalities/county municipalities must report data into KOSTRA each year, not a statistical publication itself. Both 2026 deadlines (15 and 22 Feb) have already passed relative to today (2026-08-11), so the computed next occurrences are for 2027. In practice, SSB's own annual reporting-calendar notices (e.g. NOT2025-29) sometimes shift the accounts deadline by a day or two when the stated date falls on a weekend (e.g. 23 Feb instead of 22 Feb in 2026) — actual dates should be checked against SSB's yearly KOSTRA-rapportering notice for exact business-day adjustments. Additional deadlines exist for sensitive service data (mid-January) and corrected data (mid-April, per § 6/related guidance) not captured as separate entries here.

targetReport.title: European System of Accounts 2010 (ESA 2010)
targetReport.publisher: European Parliament and Council of the European Union
targetReport.description: The EU's national accounts framework, enacted as Regulation (EU) No 549/2013. Article 1(2) sets out its two parts: 'a methodology (Annex A) on common standards, definitions, classifications and accounting rules that shall be used for compiling accounts and tables on comparable bases for the purposes of the Union' and 'a programme (Annex B) setting out the time limits by which Member States shall transmit to the Commission (Eurostat) the accounts and tables'. Unlike the international standards already in this corpus, ESA 2010 is a Regulation — member states do not adopt it by choice — which is why the EU branch was expected to produce supranational-to-national edges the Canada/US pair lacks. Annex B turned out to name tables and deadlines rather than publications; see the _dropped entries here and in eu-draft-budget.json.
targetReport.cadence_note: A generational standard, revised roughly once every fifteen to twenty years: ESA 1995 preceded it, and a further revision is already anticipated. releases_per_year matches sna-2008 (0.05) so the two read at the same pulse rate; see _open_questions.

targetReport.title: Property Assessment Notice and Assessment Roll (Current Value Assessment)
targetReport.description: Ontario's single province-wide property assessment, prepared by a not-for-profit corporation funded by all Ontario municipalities rather than by a government department. This is the structural difference from Alberta, where each municipality prepares its own roll and the province must then run an explicit equalization step to make them comparable. Ontario needs no equalization because there is one assessor. The standard is Current Value, defined in the Assessment Act s. 1(1) as 'the amount of money the fee simple, if unencumbered, would realize if sold at arm's length by a willing seller to a willing buyer'. MPAC states it uses 'one of three approaches to value properties: direct comparison approach, income approach, cost approach', with the direct comparison approach 'the most commonly used' and the choice depending on 'property type, and the number of recent comparable sales of similar properties in the area'. The returned roll and its household counts are what the Ontario Municipal Partnership Fund allocates against.
targetReport.cadence_note: The roll returns annually; the values in it have not been re-based since 2016, and the gap between those two facts is the point. The Assessment Act s. 19.2(1) sets a four-year cycle by schedule, and para 4 assigns 1 January 2016 to 'the four taxation years from 2017 to 2020'. MPAC states the schedule has been suspended: 'On August 16, 2023, the Ontario government filed a regulation to amend the Assessment Act, extending the postponement of a province-wide reassessment through the end of the 2021-2024 assessment cycle. Property assessments for the 2026 property tax year will continue to be based on fully phased-in January 1, 2016 current values.' So `releases_per_year` 1 counts the returned roll, which does move for new construction, demolition and change of use; `changes_per_year` 0.25 is the statutory reassessment cycle, which is the rate at which the valuation basis is supposed to move and has not moved in ten years. Both numbers are true and neither alone describes this node.

release_schedule.note: MPAC delivers an assessment roll annually to Ontario municipalities each Nov-Dec (with Property Assessment Notices mailed to owners with changed assessments in November, and the roll formally 'returned' in early-mid December: Dec 12 2023, Dec 10 2024, ~Dec 9 2025). This annual notice/roll cycle is distinct from the province-wide Current Value Assessment (CVA) base-year update: Ontario's Assessment Act nominally requires reassessment on a 4-year cycle, but the government has repeatedly postponed it by regulation since 2020 (most recently confirmed through the 2026 tax year), so assessed values remain frozen at January 1, 2016 current values with no announced date for the next province-wide reassessment. The annual roll-return/notice cycle, however, has continued on schedule every year regardless of the reassessment freeze.

results.basis: NARROW, AND THE NARROWNESS IS THE FINDING. Appendix F attributes six separate indicators to 'Statistics Canada' and names no release for any of them, which is agency-level attribution and the same test that removed `boc-mpr -> statcan-national-accounts` in V0.9 and killed the H.15 restoration in V0.10. Five of the six are therefore declined and recorded in _dropped. Exactly one names a publication, in Appendix G's definition of the Rural and Small Community Measure: 'The measure is based on Statistics Canada data from the 2021 Census.' That is a named recurring release and it carries this edge, alone. The basis is written this way because the edge would otherwise be read as covering all six, and a later pass finding the other five undocumented would think this edge had been demoted rather than that it had always been this narrow. STRUCTURAL NOTE: this single sentence is also the only documented link between Ontario and the rest of the corpus. Without it the two nodes in this slice would form a second connected component, breaking an invariant held since V0.8. The graph stays at one component on the strength of one clause in an appendix definition.

results.basis: The current 'Benefit Rate Adjustments' policy (last updated July 2, 2026) in the Disability Income Assistance Policy Manual states: 'AISH and ADAP benefit rates are adjusted annually, effective January 1st of each year. Starting January 1, 2026, the rate of adjustment is based on the standard escalator amount established under section 44.2 of the Alberta Personal Income Tax Act.' It adds: 'Annual benefit rate changes are calculated using the standard escalator amount established in the Alberta Personal Income Tax Act, which is the lesser of either two per cent, or the Alberta Consumer Price Index (CPI) amount from October through September year-over-year.' The policy cites as authority the AISH Act s. 3.1(2), the AISH General Regulations s. 7(3) and the Alberta Personal Income Tax Act s. 44.2. Living allowance, the modified living allowance personal allowance, the child benefit and most personal benefits are adjusted; health benefits and actual-cost benefits are not.

targetReport.title: Alberta Escalator (Alberta Personal Income Tax Act indexation factor)
targetReport.description: The annual indexation factor defined in section 44.2 of the Alberta Personal Income Tax Act and published each year by Treasury Board and Finance alongside the personal income tax bracket table. For years after 2025 it is either a percentage prescribed by regulation before January 1, or, absent a prescription, the lesser of 2% and the year-over-year change in the Alberta Consumer Price Index over the 12 months ending September 30. It is the single escalator that now drives Alberta tax brackets and credit amounts, the Alberta Child and Family Benefit, and AISH/ADAP benefit rates.
targetReport.cadence_note: One factor per taxation year, effective January 1; published in the personal income tax bracket table and in the Budget tax plan.

release_schedule.rule: If no percentage is prescribed by regulation by January 1, a CPI-derived formula (capped at 2%) applies automatically.

results.basis: Alberta Personal Income Tax Act, RSA 2000 c A-30, s. 44.2(0.1)(b) defines the Alberta escalator, absent a prescribed percentage, as the lesser of 2% and the amount determined by the formula A/B - 1, 'where A is the Consumer Price Index for Alberta for the 12-month period that ended on the last September 30 before that year, and B is the Consumer Price Index for Alberta for the 12-month period immediately preceding'. Subsection 44.2(3) then defines that index explicitly: 'the Consumer Price Index for Alberta for any 12-month period is the result arrived at by (a) aggregating the Consumer Price Index for Alberta, as published by Statistics Canada under the authority of the Statistics Act (Canada) ... for each month in that period, (b) dividing the aggregate ... by 12'.

targetReport.title: Alberta Escalator (Alberta Personal Income Tax Act indexation factor)
targetReport.description: The annual indexation factor defined in section 44.2 of the Alberta Personal Income Tax Act and published each year by Treasury Board and Finance alongside the personal income tax bracket table. It is the single escalator that now drives Alberta tax brackets and credit amounts, the Alberta Child and Family Benefit, and AISH/ADAP benefit rates.

Continuing Care (Ministerial) Regulation, Alta Reg 44/2024 under the Continuing Care Act, SA 2022, c C-26.7 -- office consolidation with amendments up to and including AR 199/2025, current as of August 27, 2025, fetched in full via a Chrome browser session (a direct fetch-tool request to the same PDF URL returns ROBOTS_DISALLOWED; the King's Printer PDF itself carries no such restriction against ordinary browser access). Section 11 in full: '11(1) In this section, “Alberta CPI” means the monthly All-items Consumer Price Index for Alberta, not seasonally adjusted, published by Statistics Canada. (2) The maximum amount of the accommodation charge set by the Minister under section 9(4) of the Act in respect of each type of accommodation must be adjusted annually on August 1 by the lesser of the following: (a) the percentage increase in the Alberta CPI for the 12-month period ending on February 28 of that year, rounded to the nearest $0.05; (b) 3.8%.' This both settles the edge and explains the number on Alberta Health's programme page: the 1.8% increase stated to take effect August 1, 2026 is the CPI figure under (a), sitting below the 3.8% cap under (b) and so the binding term. Table 6 ("Despesas Totais por Classificação Orgânica", sourced to the Ministério das Finanças' Direcção do Orçamento) itemizes multi-year expenditure by organic-classification code for all six São Tomé island district câmaras alongside the Príncipe regional government, e.g. the row "70.0.00-GRP 109 954,0 109 651,0 128 425,0 144 075,0 107 169..." through "76.0.00-CDMZ 10 950,0 14 623,7 27 966,0 32 168,0 19 966..." Code-to-name mapping (GRP = Governo Regional do Príncipe; CDAG = Câmara Distrital de Água Grande; CDCG = Câmara Distrital de Cantagalo; CDC = Câmara Distrital de Caué; CDLMB = Câmara Distrital de Lembá; CDLOBT = Câmara Distrital de Lobata; CDMZ = Câmara Distrital de Mé-Zóchi) is inferred from standard STP abbreviation convention rather than an explicit legend in the extracted text, but is corroborated by the same table's accompanying Table 8 prose, which independently names districts by percentage: "observa-se que 89% das despesas totais são de âmbito nacional, o que evidencia a abrangência das acções governamentais. results.basis: The monthly programme's industry-by-industry source table, 'National monthly gross domestic product by industry, summary of Methods and data sources' (2021), names the IPPI by title and by IMDB record number in 64 separate rows. Representative row, NAICS 3111 Animal food manufacturing, under 'Gross output': 'Sales and inventory change in constant prices, Monthly Survey of Manufacturing, Record no (number). 2101. Industrial product price indexes, Record no (number). 2318.' Record 2318 is the IPPI. `uses_data_from` follows the type already taken for statcan-gdp-monthly -> statcan-cpi, which rests on the identical evidence in the identical document. WORTH STATING PLAINLY: this is the best-evidenced deflator edge in the Canadian corpus and it was the last one built. The same table names the CPI in 27 rows and SEPH in 37, and both of those became edges two sessions before this one — the IPPI was invisible only because nobody had grepped for it. Note also that record 1301's own IMDB page never mentions the IPPI at all; the release-level disclosure lives entirely in this attached table, which is the disclosure asymmetry doctrine operating within a single statistical programme.

targetReport.title: Industrial Product Price Index (IPPI)
targetReport.description: Monthly measure of price change for major commodities sold by manufacturers operating in Canada, record 2318, produced by the Prices Division alongside the Consumer Price Index. Prices are collected at the factory gate, so they are what the producer receives rather than what a purchaser pays: record 2318 states they 'exclude all indirect taxes, such as sales taxes, customs duties and tariffs as this money does not go to the factors of production', and exclude common-carrier transport and retail or wholesale distribution beyond the gate. That is the whole reason the accounts need it as well as the CPI — the supply and use tables are built at basic prices, and the CPI measures purchasers' prices. The IPPI is the deflator the Canadian accounts actually run on: it is named in 64 rows of the monthly GDP by industry source table against the CPI's 27, and the input-output deflation guide calls it 'the main data source of deflators for manufactured goods'. Record 2318 states the role in its own words: 'the IPPI series supports the Canadian System of Macro-Economic Accounts (CSMA), where it is used in the calculation of real Gross Domestic Product (GDP).' It replaced the Industry Selling Price Index in the early 1980s.
targetReport.cadence_note: Monthly, reference period month. Two lags worth knowing before this node is used for timing. Collection: 'For most products included in the IPPI, the collection process occurs over a three-week period starting during the third week of the reference month.' Revision: 'price indexes remain subject to revision for six months after publication of a given month's data', so any dependent reading a recent month is reading a provisional number. The weighting structure moves on a far slower clock than the index — 'The entire weighting scheme for the IPPI is generally revised every 5 years' — which is what the reference period on the edge to the supply and use tables records.

results.basis: Catalogue 15F0077GIE, 'A Guide to Deflating the Input-Output Accounts: Sources and Methods' (2001), which record 1301 cites as the description of the double-deflation method used to produce constant-price GDP by industry. Under the heading 'Sources of deflators', unhedged: 'The main data source of deflators for manufactured goods is the Industrial Product Price Indexes (IPPI) produced by Statistics Canada's Prices Division. Prior to 1981, deflators were based on Industry Selling Price Indexes (ISPI).' Earlier in the same chapter, on why basic-price deflation is possible where purchaser-price deflation is not: 'the commodity price information collected by the Prices Division to compile industry product price indexes can be used to construct deflators for values at basic prices. These Industrial Product Price Indexes (IPPI), aggregated where necessary to the input-output classification, constitute the main source of deflators for manufactured commodities.' Both passages verified verbatim against the PDF. `methodology_depends_on` matches the type taken for statcan-sut -> statcan-cpi from the same document. ONE HEDGE, STATED, AND IT IS THE ONLY ONE: the guide is a 2001 edition marked ARCHIVED, twenty-five years old, and it remains the document record 1301 points at for this method. The 'can be used' softness that qualifies the CPI edge does not apply here — the 'Sources of deflators' sentence says 'is'.

results.basis: The reverse direction, and the graph's second mutual pair. Record 2318, under Estimation: 'For the IPPI, commodity and industry weights are derived from a combination of the 2019 Supply and Use Tables that closely reflect actual economic transactions by industry and the sales of goods manufactured by companies as reported for the 2019 ASML.' The same section adds that the industry indexes are 'aggregated to the level required for the input-output tables and the measurement of Gross Domestic Product', so the tables set the aggregation structure as well as the weights. Admissible under the V0.10 mutual-partner rule on its own terms: each direction is stated by a different document in its own words, each carries its own evidence_url, and the two are asymmetric in kind rather than restatements of one relationship — the tables take the IPPI as a price measure, the IPPI takes the tables as a weighting frame. `relationship_type` records the asymmetry as the rule requires: `methodology_depends_on` outbound from the tables against `uses_data_from` here, because the SUT figures are a direct numerical input to the weights rather than a method the IPPI follows. THE MECHANISM IS NOT SIMULTANEOUS AND THAT MATTERS FOR READING THE CYCLE: the 2019 tables weight today's index, and today's index deflates a later vintage of the tables. Nothing circular happens in any single calculation; the loop closes only across vintages, five years apart.

targetReport.title: Supply, Use and Input-Output Tables
targetReport.description: The annual benchmark of the Canadian System of Macroeconomic Accounts. The supply and use tables trace the production of products by domestic industries, combined with imports, through their use as intermediate inputs or as final consumption, investment or exports, and yield gross value added by industry; the symmetric industry-by-industry input-output tables are derived from them. Record 1401's own description states the tables 'can be used to calculate economy-wide gross domestic product (GDP) either directly, by summing value added over the industries, or indirectly, by summing to the economy-wide cost of primary inputs (income-based GDP) or by computing the grand total of the flow of products into final use categories (expenditure-based GDP) - the link to the national income and expenditure accounts.' Both the monthly GDP by industry programme and the quarterly income and expenditure accounts are projections off this benchmark, which is the actual shape of the Canadian accounts and was not representable in this graph until now.
targetReport.cadence_note: Annual, reference period calendar year, but with an unusually long lag: record 1401 states the tables 'are available about two and half years after the end of the reference year; this is because of the delay in obtaining the needed source data and by the complex nature of producing such a detailed account.' The programme also releases derived products on separate dates — the 2026 release schedule lists April 15 for the input-output tables, May 4 for value added in exports and June 16 for the economic impact of wireless telecommunications carriers — so releases_per_year 1 counts the benchmark tables and not the satellite products.

release_schedule.note: Statistics Canada's IMDB page for SDDS 1401 states supply/use and input-output tables are annual and 'available about two and half years after the end of the reference year' due to data-collection lag. Observed national releases: 2023 reference-year data released 2025-04-14, and 2024 reference-year data released 2026-04-15 (both via The Daily / table pid 3610008401, catalogue 15-207-X). This gives a consistent mid-April annual pattern for the most recent two cycles, implying the 2025 reference-year release would land around April 2027. Earlier years (2017-2022) show more variable timing (June-July, and some Nov/Dec releases), and there is a separate, later-lagged provincial/territorial supply-and-use table release that has landed in November in recent years (e.g. 2025-11-13 for 2022 provincial data) - so the overall SDDS 1401 program has more than one sub-release per year even though releases_per_year=1 on file; treat the April date as the primary/national release this corpus field likely tracks.

targetReport.title: North American Product Classification System (NAPCS) Canada 2022 Version 1.0
targetReport.description: The product-side counterpart to NAICS, approved as a departmental standard on 24 September 2021. It is a trilateral standard by origin — 'a joint project of the national statistical agencies of Canada, Mexico and the United States' — developed after NAICS 'to serve the same purpose but for product statistics'. Two relationships it is commonly assumed to have and does not: it is parallel to NAICS rather than derived from it, and it is explicitly NOT compatible with the UN Central Product Classification ('NAPCS Canada is not fully compatible with the CPC'). Its live connection to the accounts runs through the Supply and Use Product Classification, which its introduction states is 'largely embedded at the level of NAPCS Canada' — that is a containment relationship rather than a dependency, and the SUPC is not yet a node.
targetReport.cadence_note: Nominally a five-year revision cycle moving toward continuous update: 'Since the creation of this product classification, NAPCS Canada, has been revised on a 5-year cycle, in 2012, 2017 and 2022. NAPCS Canada was also revised in 2018 with NAPCS Canada 2017 Version 2.0, as Canada has started evolving towards adopting a permanent "evergreen" practice with regards to NAPCS, which means the updating of NAPCS Canada on an as-needed basis, with version updates between the standard 5-year revision milestones.' Four versions are named across roughly a decade — 2012, 2017, 2017 V2.0 in 2018, and 2022 — so releases_per_year is 0.4 counting published versions. changes_per_year 0.2 is the structural five-year cycle the document states.

release_schedule.rule: NAPCS Canada revisions are planned to occur every five years; the next version, NAPCS Canada 2027 Version 1.0, is scheduled for public release in February 2027.
release_schedule.note: Statistics Canada's consultation page for the NAPCS Canada 2027 revision (and the 2026 'What We Heard Report') both explicitly state a public release target of February 2027, with a preceding public notice of final approved proposals planned for February 2026 and a November 2025 notice of proposed changes. This is a documented target date (not merely a computed 5-year projection), though it is still a forward-looking schedule for a not-yet-released edition. The introduction page for NAPCS Canada 2022 (https://www.statcan.gc.ca/en/subjects/standard/napcs/2022/introduction) states revisions are 'planned to occur every five years,' consistent with the 2012->2017->2022->2027 cadence, though StatCan also issued an off-cycle Version 2.0 update in 2018 for cannabis legalization, showing the 5-year cycle is a planning target rather than a rigid rule.

results.basis: Record 1301 states the anchoring three separate ways in its own words. Under Estimation: 'The monthly estimates are benchmarked to annually chained Fisher volume indexes of GDP obtained from the constant-price supply and use tables.' Under Data accuracy: 'GDP by industry depends on the Supply and Use tables to which it is anchored', and 'as the monthly GDP by industry program relies on the annual estimates of real GDP obtained from the Supply and Use tables, the quality of these estimates has a direct influence on the quality of the monthly GDP measures.' Record 1401 says the same from the other side: 'two industry-based programs - one producing the country's current monthly GDP figures (record no. 1301), the other annual provincial-territorial estimates (record no. 1303) have been set up. These two programs, which can be viewed as extensions of the supply and use tables, use a set of indicators to project the GDP by industry benchmarks from the supply and use tables'. `calculated_from` because the monthly figure is literally a projection of a benchmark drawn from these tables, not merely informed by them — and note the release identifies the dependent by record number, which is the strongest cross-reference in the StatCan corpus so far.
results.evidenceQuote: The monthly estimates are benchmarked to annually chained Fisher volume indexes of GDP obtained from the constant-price supply and use tables.

targetReport.title: Supply, Use and Input-Output Tables
targetReport.description: The annual benchmark of the Canadian System of Macroeconomic Accounts. The supply and use tables trace the production of products by domestic industries, combined with imports, through their use as intermediate inputs or as final consumption, investment or exports, and yield gross value added by industry; the symmetric industry-by-industry input-output tables are derived from them. Record 1401's own description states the tables 'can be used to calculate economy-wide gross domestic product (GDP) either directly, by summing value added over the industries, or indirectly, by summing to the economy-wide cost of primary inputs (income-based GDP) or by computing the grand total of the flow of products into final use categories (expenditure-based GDP) - the link to the national income and expenditure accounts.' Both the monthly GDP by industry programme and the quarterly income and expenditure accounts are projections off this benchmark, which is the actual shape of the Canadian accounts and was not representable in this graph until now.
targetReport.cadence_note: Annual, reference period calendar year, but with an unusually long lag: record 1401 states the tables 'are available about two and half years after the end of the reference year; this is because of the delay in obtaining the needed source data and by the complex nature of producing such a detailed account.' The programme also releases derived products on separate dates — the 2026 release schedule lists April 15 for the input-output tables, May 4 for value added in exports and June 16 for the economic impact of wireless telecommunications carriers — so releases_per_year 1 counts the benchmark tables and not the satellite products.

results.basis: Catalogue 15F0077GIE, 'A Guide to Deflating the Input-Output Accounts: Sources and Methods' (2001), which record 1301 cites as the description of the double-deflation method used to produce constant-price GDP by industry. Chapter 2, in the passage on trade margins: 'Consumer price indexes can be used to deflate the purchaser value of commodities sold for personal expenditure. Similarly, industry product price indexes are used to deflate the basic values of the same commodities. This has made it possible to calculate the trade margin for commodities bought for personal expenditure as a residual using both of these observed prices.' `methodology_depends_on` rather than `uses_data_from` because this document is the accounts' deflation methodology and the index is named as the price measure the method takes, which is the case the type comment describes. ONE HEDGE REMAINS, AND ONE WAS RETIRED IN V0.11. Retired: the 'can be used' softness above is not the document's last word on the CPI. Four sentences later in the same passage, unhedged and read while verifying the IPPI quotations, the guide states the mechanism outright: 'The total trade margin at constant prices is calculated as the difference between the purchaser value, deflated with the appropriate Consumer Price Index (CPI), and the sum of the basic value and the ...'. 'Deflated with' is a statement of what deflates what, which is exactly what the hedged sentence was recorded as lacking, so this edge is stronger than V0.10 believed and was under-rated by a first reading that stopped at the first mention. Still standing: the guide is a 2001 edition marked ARCHIVED — it remains the document record 1301 points at for this method, but it is twenty-five years old and a later methodology note may supersede it.

results.basis: The reverse of statcan-national-accounts -> statcan-sut, and taken deliberately under the V0.10 decision that a node may be a mutual definitional partner. Record 1401, Quality evaluation: 'The input-output framework is validated for accuracy, coherence and overall reasonableness. The major components of the framework, such as the income and expenditure-based GDP components are reconciled to the national and provincial-territorial income and expenditure accounts.' Record 1901 states the converse in its own Estimation section: 'The annual benchmarks for GDP by the income approach and by the expenditure approach are generated through the construction of annual supply and use tables which balance the supply of each product in the economy against its use.' Neither statement is a mistake and neither supersedes the other — annual benchmarking is an iterative balancing process in which each side constrains the other, which is what the accounts mean by coherence. The pair is asymmetric in strength and the `relationship_type` records that: 1901 discloses the SUT as the source of its benchmark levels (`calculated_from`), while 1401 describes reconciliation as a validation step rather than an input (`methodology_depends_on`), so the cycle is not symmetric in weight and does not assert that the two are interchangeable.

release_schedule.rule: Under the FFIEC/FDIC/OCC/Federal Reserve interagency Call Report instructions, banks without foreign offices (FFIEC 041/051 filers) must submit within 30 calendar days after the report (quarter-end) date; banks with foreign offices (FFIEC 031 filers, more than one foreign office) get 35 calendar days. If the calculated due date falls on a weekend or holiday, the deadline moves to the next business day.
release_schedule.note: Call Reports are filed quarterly for report (as-of) dates March 31, June 30, September 30, and December 31. The Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis's bank-supervision page lists explicit deadlines through Q3 2026 (confirmed: Dec 31 2025 report due Fri Jan 30 2026 -- verified directly against FDIC's own FIL for Q4 2025 -- and Sept 30 2026 report due Fri Oct 30 2026). The Q4 2026 entry (Dec 31, 2026 report) was not yet listed on any source as of Aug 2026 (FDIC/FFIEC typically publish the FIL for a quarter only after that quarter closes), so I computed it myself: 30 days after Dec 31, 2026 is Jan 30, 2027, which falls on a Saturday, so under the standard weekend-rollover rule the deadline would move to Monday, Feb 1, 2027 -- this specific date is my computation (implied), not yet published by the agencies. The Q2 2026 report (June 30, 2026) was already due July 30, 2026, which is in the past relative to 2026-08-11, so it is omitted.

targetReport.title: Local Government: The Urban Government Act No. 8 of 1969
targetReport.description: Eswatini's (then Swaziland's) foundational urban-municipal-finance statute. Part IX ('Municipal Funds'), Section 86 ('Revenues of the council'): 'The revenues of a council shall consist of-- (a) all rates lawfully levied by the council; ... (g) all moneys paid to the council by the Government as contributions, grants, endowment or otherwise, except where such moneys are paid with a condition as to the purpose for which such moneys are paid...' -- establishing government grants as one permitted category of council revenue, though the Act itself states no allocation formula or percentage; the actual subvention/CIP-grant amounts are set by later Ministry of Housing administrative practice (see sz-mohud-annual-report-2024-25). Section 57(1) separately grants own-source fee authority: 'a council may charge fees for any service or facility provided by it or for any licence or permit issued by it.' HOSTING/QUALITY CAVEAT: this PDF is hosted by Gender Links (genderlinks.org.za), a South African NGO, not an Eswatini-government domain -- no official gov.sz/legislation portal copy could be located (the gov.sz 'ACTS' resources page does not list it). It is nonetheless authentic statutory text; its section numbering is independently corroborated by the Ministry of Housing's FY2024/25 report, which separately cites 'Section 115' and 'Section 8' of the same Act. The scanned/OCR'd PDF also has significant digit-garbling errors (e.g. '35.' for '85.', '36.' for '86.', page-footer range markers like 'ss.85-87' confirming the correct numbering despite garbled in-body digits); the quotes above are reproduced in cleaned form.

The IMF's own page for this report is titled 'Update of the Consumer Price Index Manual' and explains the 2020 edition was produced because 'methods and best practices have continued to evolve' since 2004, following requests from the 2014 UNECE-ILO CPI Experts Meeting -- i.e., updates are triggered by inter-agency expert consensus, not a fixed schedule. targetReport.title: EAC Regulations for Compiling Harmonised Consumer Price Indices (HCPI)
targetReport.description: A binding East African Community instrument (March 2022) requiring Partner States to compile and submit a Harmonised CPI to the EAC Secretariat, for regional comparability and East African Monetary Union convergence-criteria monitoring -- described as binding in its entirety and directly applicable, and classification 'shall be based on the most recent official United Nations Classification of Individual Consumption According to Purpose (COICOP)'. Filed `supranational` rather than `international` on the same reasoning the corpus already applies to the EU's ESA 2010: a regional body legislating a binding, directly-applicable obligation, not a standard adopted by choice. Distinct from Kenya's own domestic CPI, which aligns with these regulations' spirit (per KNBS's own rebasing report) without the regulations themselves directly governing the domestic release -- the binding obligation is to also produce the separate HCPI submission.

release_schedule.note: This is a one-off legal/regulatory instrument (EAC Regulations for Compiling Harmonised Consumer Price Indices, published March 2022), not a recurring statistical publication. The document itself was 'gazetted' with a target entry-into-force date of 31 Dec 2024 (Article 106), a one-time milestone, not a recurring cycle. Internally it does specify review cycles for the underlying CPI methodology (weights reviewed at max 5-year intervals per Art. 704.1, mini-surveys every 2-3 years per Art. 704.2, EAC-level weights every 3-5 years per Art. 706.5, annual compliance reports per Art. 113.3), but none of these are a stated periodicity for reissuing or amending the Regulations document itself. There is no found evidence of a fixed amendment/republication cadence for the Regulations text, so releases_per_year probably should not be treated as a fixed number for this report at all -- it is better modeled as irregular (amended only when the EAC Council/Secretariat decides to revise it) rather than assigned any specific interval.

targetReport.title: Public Service Social Security Fund Act, 2018 (Cap. 371)
targetReport.description: VERIFIED DIRECTLY this session (R.E. 2023 consolidated text). Tanzania's main public-service pension statute, named by the National Social Protection Policy 2023 among its governing instruments (see dependency below). Read section-by-section for any inflation/CPI adjustment mechanism: s.30 (Rates of retirement pension) sets the calculation formula but delegates specifics to regulations, with no automatic adjustment clause; s.34 (Rate of invalidity pension) likewise delegates to regulations without mentioning review; ss.25-48 (Benefits under the Scheme) cover qualification, eligibility and payment procedure with no periodic-adjustment provision; s.57 (Actuarial valuation report) requires triennial valuations directed at fund soundness, not benefit levels; s.58 (Restoration of financial soundness) addresses deficit recovery, not indexation. The one adjustment-adjacent power found is s.18(4), letting the Minister adjust contribution rates 'taking into consideration of the actuarial valuation' -- a fund-solvency lever, not a benefit-indexation one, and confined to contributions rather than paid pensions. No CPI or inflation-linked benefit-adjustment provision exists anywhere in the Act -- confirming, at primary-statute level, the Policy's own admission (tz-national-social-protection-policy-2023) that no such mechanism exists.

results.basis: SSA states the statutory formula outright: 'The Social Security Act specifies a formula for determining each COLA. According to the formula, COLAs are based on increases in the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers (CPI-W). CPI-Ws are calculated on a monthly basis by the Bureau of Labor Statistics. A COLA effective for December of the current year is equal to the percentage increase (if any) in the CPI-W from the average for the third quarter of the current year to the average for the third quarter of the last year in which a COLA became effective.' The arithmetic is shown in full: the 2.8 percent COLA effective December 2025 is (317.265 - 308.729) / 308.729 x 100, using the July, August and September CPI-W values for 2024 and 2025. Note the index is CPI-W, a subpopulation index for urban wage earners and clerical workers, not the headline CPI-U.

results.basis: The Handbook of Methods is unambiguous that the survey cannot produce population levels by itself: 'Population controls are independent estimates of the population that are used to weight the CPS sample results so that estimates reflect the civilian noninstitutional population ages 16 and older. The Census Bureau develops the CPS population controls, which are based on decennial census population counts, supplemented with birth and death data and estimates of net international migration. The Census Bureau reviews and adjusts the population estimates every year. BLS introduces the Census Bureau's annual population control adjustments into CPS estimates for January.' This is why the January Employment Situation carries a break in the household series each year — the level jumps by whatever the new vintage says, independent of anything that happened in the labour market.

targetReport.publisher: US Census Bureau and US Bureau of Labor Statistics
targetReport.description: The monthly household survey of about 60,000 eligible households, collected by the Census Bureau and estimated by BLS. Proc. 2025-32 says the figures 'are generally determined by reference to § 1(f)', and 26 U.S.C. § 1(f) names the index and the reference period exactly: '(3)(A) The cost-of-living adjustment for any calendar year is the percentage (if any) by which (i) the C-CPI-U for the preceding calendar year, exceeds (ii) the CPI for calendar year 2016, multiplied by the amount determined under subparagraph (B).' '(6)(A) The term "C-CPI-U" means the Chained Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (as published by the Bureau of Labor Statistics of the Department of Labor). The values ... shall be the latest values so published as of the date on which such Bureau publishes the initial value of the Chained Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers for the month of August for the preceding calendar year.' '(6)(B) The C-CPI-U for any calendar year is the average of the C-CPI-U as of the close of the 12-month period ending on August 31 of such calendar year.' The August cut-off is why the IRS can publish next year's brackets in October, and the freeze on 'latest values as of' the initial August release is how the statute copes with the fact that the chained index is revised for a year after first publication.

targetReport.title: Chained Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (C-CPI-U)
targetReport.description: A superlative price index built from the same price quotes as the CPI-U but using a Tornqvist formula with expenditure weights from both the current and the comparison period, so it captures consumers substituting between categories as relative prices change. It therefore rises more slowly than the CPI-U. Published monthly alongside the CPI, but initially as an estimate: values are revised twice and only become final about a year later, which is why the tax code pins the values used to those published as of the initial August release.
targetReport.cadence_note: Released with the monthly CPI news release, but each month's value is initial and subject to three interim revisions, with final data posted 10 to 12 months later.

results.basis: The chained index is not a separate collection — it is the CPI's own price quotes reaggregated. BLS: 'all three of the CPI indexes are built in two stages. In the first stage, prices for each of the 7,776 item-area combinations (243 item categories X 32 geographic areas) are averaged together to form 7,776 basic indexes... The geometric mean estimator is used in the C-CPI-U in the same item categories in which it is used in the CPI-U and CPI-W. In the second stage... It is at this second stage where the C-CPI-U is different from the CPI-U and CPI-W. The use of a superlative formula for upper-level aggregation... is designed to address consumer substitution across item categories.' BLS also confirms the policy use: 'Since 2017, the C-CPI-U has been used to adjust Federal tax brackets for inflation.' The average gap is about 0.2 percentage points a year, which compounds.

targetReport.title: Constitution of the Republic of South Africa, 1996 — Chapter 13 (Finance)
targetReport.description: The constitutional basis for how revenue is split among South Africa's three spheres of government. VERIFIED DIRECTLY this session. s.213: money raised nationally goes into the National Revenue Fund, and 'a province's equitable share of revenue raised nationally' is 'a direct charge against the National Revenue Fund'. s.214(1)(a): 'An Act of Parliament must provide for... the equitable division of revenue raised nationally among the national, provincial and local spheres of government'; s.214(2) lists the factors that Act must weigh, including provinces' and municipalities' ability to 'provide basic services' and 'fiscal capacity and efficiency'. s.226 gives each province its own Revenue Fund; s.227(1)(a) entitles local government and provinces to 'an equitable share of revenue raised nationally... to provide basic services'. ss.228-229 give provinces and municipalities limited own-revenue powers (no income tax, VAT or customs duty for either).

System of National Accounts 2008 (SNA 2008), published jointly by the European Commission, International
Monetary Fund, Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development, United Nations, and World Bank. targetReport.title: Social Security (Minimum Standards) Convention, 1952 (No. 102)
targetReport.description: The ILO's foundational treaty setting minimum standards across nine branches of social security, including unemployment benefit. VERIFIED DIRECTLY this session that South Africa has NOT ratified this Convention -- the ILO's own site (March 2026 workshop article) describes South Africa as still assessing the feasibility of ratification against a comparative legal analysis, not as a ratifying state. The Unemployment Insurance Act nonetheless names it by name as the benchmark for the Minister's discretionary Gazette-notice power to adjust the benefit scale (s.12(3)(a)) -- a domestic statute voluntarily referencing an unratified international instrument as a reference point, not a treaty-driven obligation. Filed with an INT country code and international jurisdiction level per the schema's existing convention for standards bodies.
targetReport.cadence_note: A single 1952 instrument, not revised since; releases_per_year is nominal so the pulse rate reads as near-static, matching the treatment of sna-2008 and the cpi-manual node.

release_schedule.note: This is the text of an ILO Convention (a treaty adopted in 1952, still in force) — a one-off foundational legal instrument, not a recurring statistical/government publication. The convention text itself is not re-released on any cadence. What does recur is member states' Article 22 reporting obligation: ratifying states must submit periodic reports on measures taken to give effect to the Convention, and per ILO's supervisory system, Convention 102 is classified as a 'technical convention', so reports are formally called for on a 6-year cycle, staggered across 6 alphabetical groups of member states (so different countries report on C102 in different years). There is no single global 'next release' date this produces — it's a rolling, country-by-country reporting obligation, not a dated publication event. Treating this corpus entry as having a fixed releases_per_year is therefore not really meaningful; it should probably be flagged as irregular/non-recurring rather than assigned a numeric cadence.
